qs.q: A 25-year-old male is admitted with a cervical spine fracture. Which of the following injury levels would result in fatal respiratory failure without immediate mechanical ventilation due to involvement of the phrenic nerve?
o: Levels C5–C6
Levels C1–C2
Levels T3–T5
Levels C7–T1
qs.e: The phrenic nerve arises from C3 to C5, meaning injuries above C3 are fatal without ventilation. C1 to C2 injuries are well above this critical threshold.
qs.s: Spinal Cord Injury: Assessment, Spinal Shock and Management: MCQs

qs.q: A patient sustained a severe spinal injury, and the surgical team is evaluating indications for operative intervention based on Denis's classification. What constitutes an unstable thoracolumbar spine fracture?
o: Damage confined to the posterior spinous process alone
Isolated fracture of a single transverse process
Fracture that compromises two or more spinal columns
Injury restricted solely to the anterior column
qs.e: According to Denis's classification, injury to two or more columns (or involvement of the middle column) makes a fracture unstable. Isolated single column or process fractures are generally stable.
qs.s: Spinal Cord Injury: Assessment, Spinal Shock and Management: MCQs

qs.q: A 40-year-old driver presents with an odontoid fracture through the base of the dens following a high-speed crash. Which classification type is this, and what is its clinical significance?
o: Type I – tip avulsion, heals well with a cervical collar
Type III – involves the body, associated with high brain‑stem compression mortality
Type IV – rare variant necessitating emergency laminectomy
Type II – fracture at the base, most common and highest risk of non‑union
qs.e: Type II odontoid fractures occur through the base, are the commonest, and carry the worst prognosis for non-union. Type I is a tip avulsion, which heals well in a collar.
qs.s: Spinal Cord Injury: Assessment, Spinal Shock and Management: MCQs

qs.q: A patient is evaluated after an axial loading injury to the head, and imaging reveals a four-part burst fracture of the ring of C1. What is the characteristic feature of this specific injury?
o: Neurological injury is uncommon because the spinal canal is wide at this level
High frequency of severe initial neurological deficit due to narrow canal
Involves disruption of the middle and posterior columns exclusively
Always requires emergency anterior corpectomy and fusion
qs.e: A Jefferson fracture is a burst fracture of the ring of C1 from axial loading; because the spinal canal is wide at this level, neurological injury is uncommon. It is typically managed with a halo vest or collar.

qs.q: A 55-year-old man is admitted following a motor vehicle collision with multiple rib fractures and a right-sided flail chest. He is intubated and placed on mechanical ventilation. Two hours later, he develops sudden severe hypotension, absent breath sounds on the right hemithorax, and tracheal deviation to the left. What is the immediate best next step in management?
o: Immediate insertion of a central venous catheter
Emergency bedside bronchoscopy
Urgent administration of noradrenaline infusion
Needle decompression of the right chest
qs.e: The patient has developed a tension pneumothorax, a life-threatening obstructive shock secondary to barotrauma from positive pressure ventilation. Immediate needle decompression or chest tube insertion is required before any diagnostic imaging.
qs.s: Surgical Critical Care: ICU, Respiratory Failure, Ventilation, Blood: MCQs

qs.q: A 30-year-old male sustains a closed tibial shaft fracture following a motorcycle crash. Eight hours later, he develops severe, disproportionate pain in his lower leg that worsens with passive toe extension, alongside tense, wooden compartments. What is the fundamental pathophysiology causing muscle and nerve necrosis in this condition?
o: Bacterial superinfection of the deep fascial planes
Primary arterial laceration leading to immediate distal gangrene
Direct thermal injury to the epimysium from the fracture hematoma
Elevated intracompartmental pressure causing venous obstruction and capillary collapse
qs.e: Acute compartment syndrome occurs when a rise in pressure within a closed osteofascial compartment exceeds venous pressure, leading to venous obstruction, capillary collapse, and subsequent ischaemia. Arterial laceration causes different ischemic syndromes rather than isolated intercompartmental pressure elevation.
qs.s: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome, Peritoneal Adhesions and Compartment: MCQs

qs.q: A 7-year-old child is hit by a car and sustains a closed head injury. A computed tomography (CT) scan reveals a skull fracture where a bone fragment is displaced inward. Under which specific condition is surgical elevation indicated for this type of fracture?
o: The child develops a transient period of amnesia
The fracture line crosses a meningeal vascular groove
The fracture is located over the temporal bone
The depression exceeds the thickness of the skull
qs.e: Surgical elevation of a depressed skull fracture is indicated if the depression is more than the thickness of the skull or twice the thickness of the table, if it is compound, or if there are neurological signs.
qs.s: Head Injury: Assessment, Intracranial Haematomas and Management of: MCQs

qs.q: A 45-year-old man falls from a roof and sustains a basal skull fracture. Which clinical finding is characteristic of this specific type of skull injury?
o: A crescentic subdural hypodense collection over the convexity
A shearing injury of white matter tracts with normal initial CT
Periorbital ecchymosis and cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhoea
A biconvex extra-axial hyperdense mass on CT scan
qs.e: Basal skull fractures characteristically present with CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea, periorbital ecchymosis ('raccoon eyes'), and mastoid ecchymosis ('Battle's sign'). Biconvex hyperdense masses represent extradural haematomas.
qs.s: Head Injury: Assessment, Intracranial Haematomas and Management of: MCQs

es.q: Outline the stages and key features of fracture healing.
es.m:
- **0–1 day (Hematoma formation):** Fibrin mesh seals the site; platelets release PDGF, TGF-β, and FGF to activate osteoprogenitor cells.
- **0–2 weeks (Soft callus):** Osteoprogenitor cells proliferate, depositing woven bone trabeculae subperiosteally while fibrocartilage and hyaline cartilage form.
- **2–3 weeks (Bony callus):** Endochondral ossification converts cartilage to bone, bridges the fracture ends, stiffens the callus, and permits weight bearing.
- **3 weeks–months (Remodeling):** Woven bone is replaced by lamellar bone, the medullary cavity is restored, and excess callus is resorbed.
- **Complications:** Poor healing can result in delayed union, nonunion leading to pseudoarthros

ai.subject: Surgery
ai.summary: A fracture is a break in the continuity of bone. Diagnosis involves history, physical exam, and imaging. Management focuses on pain control, immobilisation, and restoring function, with surgery for complex cases.

sections.p: A fracture is a disruption in the continuity of a bone. Clinical diagnosis relies on a history of trauma, characteristic pain, swelling, deformity, and limited function. Imaging is crucial for confirmation and characterisation.

Fracture severity is classified by displacement, comminution (number of fragments), and whether the skin is broken (open vs. closed). Open fractures are graded using the Gustilo-Anderson classification based on wound size and contamination.
b: Open (compound) fracture: bone communicates with the external environment.
Displaced fracture: bone fragments are out of alignment.
Comminuted fracture: bone is broken into multiple pieces.

sections.p: Trauma is the most common cause, ranging from direct blows to falls. Pathological fractures occur through weakened bone due to conditions like osteoporosis, tumours, or infections. Stress fractures result from repetitive force.

Patients typically present with acute pain at the site of injury, often exacerbated by movement. Swelling, bruising, and visible deformity may be present. In open fractures, the bone may be visible, and there is a risk of contamination.
b: Inability to bear weight or use the affected limb.
Bleeding or exposed bone in open fractures.

t.b: To confirm the presence, location, and type of fracture. Shows displacement, angulation, and comminution. Essential for diagnosis and initial management planning. If unavailable, clinical assessment guides initial management.
To better visualise complex fractures, joint involvement, or comminution, especially for surgical planning. Provides detailed cross-sectional anatomy. Useful when X-rays are inconclusive.
To assess associated soft tissue injuries (ligaments, tendons, nerves, blood vessels) and occult fractures not visible on X-ray. Useful for suspected stress fractures or spinal injuries.

To assess for anaemia, electrolyte imbalances, and calcium levels, especially in elderly patients or those with suspected pathological fractures or significant blood loss. Helps identify underlying metabolic bone disease.

sections.p: Urgent attention is needed for open fractures, signs of neurovascular compromise, or suspected pelvic/femoral fractures due to high risk of bleeding. Complications include infection, non-union, malunion, compartment syndrome, and nerve/vessel damage.
b: Signs of neurovascular compromise (absent pulses, paraesthesia, paralysis).
Suspected pelvic or femur fracture (risk of haemorrhage).
Compartment syndrome (swelling causing pressure on nerves/vessels).

sections.p: Initial management involves pain relief and immobilisation. Definitive treatment depends on fracture type and location, ranging from casting to surgical fixation. Open fractures require urgent wound debridement and antibiotics.
b: Analgesia (e.g., paracetamol, NSAIDs, opioids) for pain control.
Immobilisation (splinting, casting) to promote healing and reduce pain.
Reduction (manipulation) of displaced fractures to restore alignment.
Surgical fixation (plates, screws, rods) for unstable or complex fractures.
Antibiotics for open fractures to prevent infection.

sections.p: Follow-up includes serial X-rays to monitor healing and ensure alignment is maintained. Prevention focuses on reducing fall risk, managing osteoporosis, and using appropriate protective equipment during sports.
b: Physiotherapy to regain strength and mobility.
Management of osteoporosis (calcium, vitamin D, bisphosphonates).

sections.p: Fractures can be mistaken for severe sprains, dislocations, or contusions, especially in the absence of obvious deformity or displacement on initial examination.

A normal X-ray does not exclude a fracture, particularly stress fractures or occult fractures, where clinical suspicion should prompt further investigation or close follow-up. Soft tissue swelling can obscure fracture lines.
b: Normal X-ray in the presence of significant pain and tenderness.
Early post-injury swelling obscuring fracture details.
Stress fractures may not be visible on initial imaging.

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of nerve damage (numbness, tingling, paralysis).
Signs of poor circulation (pale, cold limb, absent pulse).

faq.q: What is the most common cause of fractures?
faq.a: Trauma, such as falls or direct blows, is the most common cause of fractures in most age groups.

faq.q: How long does a fracture take to heal?
faq.a: Healing time varies greatly depending on the bone, fracture type, age, and overall health, but typically ranges from 6-8 weeks for simple fractures in young adults.

faq.q: Can a fracture heal without a cast?
faq.a: Some stable, non-displaced fractures may heal with just immobilisation via splinting or functional bracing, but many require casting or surgical intervention.
